title: Menlo Ventures' Deedy Das Flags Scaling Cracks as Kimi K3 Buckles Under Its Own Weight
excerpt: The world's largest open-weight AI model forced Moonshot to pause subscriptions within 48 hours of launch, spotlighting the fragile economics of trillion-parameter systems that Indian-origin investor Deedy Das and other Silicon Valley voices have warned about.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Moonshot AI paused Kimi K3 subscriptions just 48 hours post-launch due to overwhelming demand.
  • Deedy Das warns that open-weight AI models face unsustainable economics at large scales.
  • Kimi K3's operating costs are high despite being cheaper than OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol.
  • The Kimi K3 launch echoes past market disruptions, raising questions about AI's economic foundations.
Kimi K3's Launch and Impact
›Kimi K3 launched on July 17, 2025.
›Subscriptions paused on July 20, 2025.
›Model features 2.8 trillion parameters.
›User demand exceeded GPU cluster capacity.
  • Moonshot AI paused new subscriptions for Kimi K3 on July 20, just two days after launching the 2.8 trillion-parameter model, after user demand overwhelmed its GPU clusters.
  • Indian-origin Menlo Ventures partner Deedy Das, an early Anthropic backer, has been a leading voice warning that open-weight models face brutal economics at frontier scale — a thesis Kimi K3's capacity crunch now validates.
  • Kimi K3 is priced at 40% less than OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, but its massive parameter count makes it prohibitively expensive to self-host, undermining the core promise of open-weight AI.
  • The episode echoes the January 2025 DeepSeek moment that wiped nearly $1 trillion from U.S. tech stocks, though Wall Street's reaction has been more measured this time.

Moonshot AI, the Beijing-based startup backed by Alibaba Group, was forced to halt new consumer subscriptions for its Kimi K3 model on Sunday — barely 48 hours after unveiling what it called the world's largest open-weight artificial intelligence system. User demand had "sharply exceeded forecasts" and was "approaching the limits of existing clusters," the company said.

The capacity crunch has given ammunition to investors and analysts who have questioned whether building ever-larger open models is economically sustainable. Among the most prominent sceptics is Debarghya "Deedy" Das, the Kolkata-born partner at Menlo Ventures who helped lead the firm's investment in Anthropic and manages its $100 million Anthology Fund for AI startups.

The Open-Weight Paradox

Das, who grew up in Kolkata before studying computer science at Cornell and working on Google Search, has emerged as one of Silicon Valley's most influential voices on the structural economics of AI. In public commentary and industry appearances, he has consistently argued that while open-weight models democratise access to AI capabilities, they face a fundamental tension: the very scale that makes them competitive with closed-source rivals also makes them punishingly expensive to serve.

Kimi K3 illustrates that tension in stark terms. At 2.8 trillion parameters, it is the first open-weight model to approach the 3-trillion-parameter mark. It features a 1-million-token context window and uses a sparse mixture-of-experts architecture with 896 experts, activating only 16 per task. Third-party evaluator Arena.ai ranked it first in web interface-building, while Vals AI placed it second overall behind only Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.

"Kimi K3 has received far more love than we expected, and our GPUs are feeling it."

— Moonshot AI, via X

But that scale comes at a cost. Ryan Fedasiuk, a fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, noted that running the model locally would require "hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of computing equipment." Max Weinbach of Creative Strategies pointed out that operating Kimi K3 well requires Nvidia's Blackwell-generation GB200 or GB300 racks, which cost $4 million to $6 million each.

A Pattern Das Has Been Tracking

Das's scepticism about the sustainability of open-model economics predates Kimi K3. In his widely followed commentary on X, where he has over 200,000 followers, and LinkedIn, he has analysed how the AI industry's value is concentrating among a handful of players — OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Nvidia and Meta — while the costs of competing at the frontier spiral upward.

As a partner at Menlo Ventures, which has invested $1 billion in Anthropic and recently raised a record $3 billion fund, Das occupies a unique vantage point. His firm's thesis is that closed-model companies with deep pockets and proprietary distribution — ChatGPT's product ecosystem, Claude's enterprise integrations — will retain pricing power even as open-weight alternatives close the benchmark gap.

Kimi K3's subscription freeze appears to support that view. Moonshot acknowledged it would split future memberships into two tiers, including a dedicated coding plan, to better match compute resources with demand — an implicit admission that the one-size-fits-all approach cannot sustain the model's inference costs.

Market Ripples and Geopolitical Undertones

The episode arrives at a sensitive moment for AI markets. When Moonshot unveiled Kimi K3 on July 17, shares of Chinese AI competitors Zhipu and MiniMax plunged 27.7% and 16.5% respectively in Hong Kong. The iShares Semiconductor ETF fell 1.6% on Friday, while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.4%.

"For markets, the headline is simple: Investors are starting to question whether the U.S. maintains the same commanding lead in AI that many had assumed over the last 18 months," wrote Mizuho Securities managing director Daniel O'Regan.

Harrison Rolfes, a private markets analyst at PitchBook, offered a blunter assessment: "Kimi-K3 is essentially the spark hitting a room already filled with gas. If intelligence gets cheaper faster than expected, the justification for hyperscalers pouring hundreds of billions into data centres loses its floor."

The parallels to the January 2025 DeepSeek moment are impossible to ignore. Back then, DeepSeek's R1 model triggered one of the largest single-day market-value losses in Wall Street history. This time, the sell-off has been more contained — but the questions it raises about AI's economic foundations are, if anything, more pointed.

Diaspora Angle: From Kolkata to the AI Power Table

Das's trajectory — from Kolkata to Cornell to Google to Glean (where he was part of the founding team that scaled the enterprise AI company to a $7 billion valuation) to one of the youngest partners at a top-tier VC firm — has made him a prominent figure in Silicon Valley's Indian diaspora. His promotion to partner at Menlo Ventures in September 2025 was widely covered in Indian business media, and he has been vocal about the opportunities he sees for Indian engineers and entrepreneurs in the AI boom.

His perspective on Kimi K3 carries weight precisely because Menlo Ventures has skin in the game on the other side of the equation. As an early and significant Anthropic backer, the firm's returns depend partly on closed-model companies maintaining their competitive moat. Das's analysis of open-model fragility is both an investor thesis and a market prediction — one that Kimi K3's operational stumble has made considerably harder to dismiss.

What Comes Next

Moonshot is pressing ahead. The company plans to release Kimi K3's full model weights by July 27 and is preparing for a potential Hong Kong IPO, having engaged Goldman Sachs and China International Capital Corp as financial advisers, according to Reuters. Its valuation reached $30 billion in June, up from $20 billion just weeks earlier.

Meanwhile, the capacity arms race intensifies. Alibaba announced on Sunday that Qwen3.8-Max-Preview, its own 2.4-trillion-parameter model, had debuted on its AI platforms ahead of a planned open-weight release. U.S. export controls on advanced Nvidia chips continue to constrain Chinese AI firms' access to computing power — a bottleneck that makes capacity crunches like Kimi K3's all the more likely to recur.

For Das and the investors watching from Silicon Valley, the lesson may be straightforward: in AI, being the biggest is not the same as being sustainable.
